body.text: This week the McKinnon Institute had planned to publish its second annual index tracking the health of Australian democracy. Last year’s inaugural index served as a depressing baseline for anyone wanting our democratic system to survive and thrive.

Based on a survey of more than 4000 people, it showed trust in federal parliamentarians was alarmingly low, at 36 per cent, and less than half of respondents were happy with the country’s direction. The first update of that benchmark was scheduled for Wednesday.
“We’ll see what has shifted, what hasn’t, and whether some of last year’s warning signs are becoming something more serious,” McKinnon’s pre-release statement said.

Respondents to the McKinnon survey are asked for their reactions to a series of statements, including: “Australia’s federal politicians understand and represent people like me.” Last year, more than half disagreed. Less than half believed federal politicians could be trusted to do the right thing, showed empathy and were honest. Almost 46 per cent said their trust in federal politicians was low.

After independent MP Helen Haines was rammed by a four-wheel-drive in the street outside her Wangaratta electorate office on Monday afternoon, the foundation cancelled plans to unveil this year’s findings and rescheduled for early next month. Given that a forty-three-year-old local man is facing a string of charges over the allegedly deliberate attack and sixty-five-year-old Haines has had both legs amputated and is fighting for life in hospital, it was an understandable decision. The motive for the alleged attack is unclear.

We know from McKinnon’s 2025 index that three-quarters of respondents backed democracy but less than half were satisfied with how it was working. Flagging the coming update, the institute’s summary of last year’s findings also makes eerie reading under the circumstances.

“People outside our major cities were less likely to believe the political system gave them a say,” it said. “Younger Australians were more open to political violence and less comfortable maintaining friendships across political divides. Around one in six Australians told us their main reason for voting was to avoid a fine.”
It teased this year’s findings, which it said would reveal whether “another year of elections, political debate and government decisions” had shifted how Australians view democracy.

“We won’t give away the results just yet, but we can say this: Australia’s democratic report card hasn’t suddenly turned around,” McKinnon’s statement said. “The warning lights we saw last year are still flashing, and some may be getting brighter.”

Written before Monday’s events, the flashing-lights metaphor was horribly prescient. So, too, were comments made back in August by Licia Heath, chief executive officer of the non-partisan organisation Women for Election, which helps encourage and equip women considering a political career. Discussing the findings of a survey of Australian female politicians about their experiences of online abuse, Heath said the abuse had “massively amplified” in the past two years and she feared where it was leading. “I’m genuinely scared that we’re going to wait till a woman is killed in public office in this country until we get in front of the issues,” she said on 12 August.

The report found 88 per cent of women surveyed had experienced online abuse or intimidation linked to their political involvement and 76 per cent believed the problem had worsened since 2024. Younger women and those in local government reported higher levels of abuse than those who were older and those involved in state and federal politics. Half of all women who had experienced the abuse said they weren’t sure they would run again and 64 per cent said it had made them less inclined to stay involved, to seek higher office or to encourage other women.

At the same Parliament House event, the chair of the University of London’s Centre for Journalism and Democracy, Australian journalist Julie Posetti, cited the murders of British Labour MP Jo Cox ten years ago and former British Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe in July this year and said Australian surveys recorded a trajectory of abuse similar to those in other countries.
She and Heath both expressed concern that those examples and the volume of abuse Australian female MPs and councillors were reporting would drive women out of politics.

Posetti called for an urgent interagency effort to try to stem the abuse, stop it tipping into violence and prevent the retrograde exodus. Regulators, law-enforcement, educators and others needed to work together using the kind of cross-parliamentary cooperation that occurred during the Covid-19 emergency as a model.
“The tinderbox is real here, and the action needs to be rapid,” Posetti said. “And I would regard this as a threat to Australian democracy on a scale that is pandemic-like.”

Female parliamentarians face significantly more threats of violence than their male counterparts but the threats to all politicians have escalated, especially recently. Security agencies report an average of one prosecution a week connected to threats made to holders of political office in Australia but emphasise that some people resorting to violence have given no sign previously of that possibility. In recent weeks, police have warned MPs and media executives privately that the reported incidence of threatening behaviour was at levels that suggested some kind of attack was likely.

It’s been noted extensively since Monday that the alleged attack on Helen Haines was the most violent incident involving a politician in Australia since the assassination of New South Wales state Labor MP John Newman in 1994.

The historical reference is relevant to the dangers parliamentarians face but there’s a significant difference between the two events, beyond the first being fatal. Newman was targeted by an organised crime gang. The alleged attack on Helen Haines involved a local man from a family she knew. It highlights the complex mix of circumstances in 2026 that makes the danger to political representatives greater and even harder to pinpoint: global instability, acute financial pressures, mental health issues and the impact of technology designed to amplify grievance and reward outrage.

Making matters worse, that technology both isolates and connects people, disrupts their ability to reason and forces politicians to engage constantly. As a result, they now face threats from everywhere and anyone, all the time.

For federal MPs, this common danger was a unifier as they tried to grasp what had occurred to Helen Haines. If it could happen to her, who is among the least provocative and pugnacious in their ranks, it could happen to any of them.

It may be thirty-two years since John Newman’s murder but other events since then have prompted the same kind of self-reflection and pleas to consider the human toll of politics. A federal Labor senator tried to take his own life in 1997 under sustained pressure over travel expenses. In 2005, amid a storm of publicity around personal behaviour, a prominent Liberal in the NSW state parliament attempted the same. In 2000, after experiencing acute personal stress from a relationship breakdown, forty-four-year-old Victorian Labor MP Greg Wilton ended his life.

These were not physical attacks by others but they did prompt parliamentarians to reflect on what they could have done and how they should behave in future. In the condolence motion for Wilton, then prime minister John Howard laid down a challenge to the whole parliament.

“Ultimately the responsibility is ours,” Howard said. “We must wear the responsibility for looking after each other. We are a political family, irrespective of our politics. In some respects I think we are a family that lets itself down.”

Twenty-six years on, in very different times and circumstances, another shocking event has given politicians pause. A special parliamentary debate has been scheduled for Monday next week to pay tribute to Haines as she battles what are still life-threatening injuries. The contributions there will doubtless touch on similar themes.

Yes, the news of Monday’s incident united political rivals in shock and distress and started a public conversation about these dangerous days, the loss of civility and the need to work harder to mend a fraying social fabric. But by week’s end, it had given way to partisan brawling about hypocritical behaviour that contradicted calls to be better.

That brings to mind the lament of another independent MP during another of the many rancorous episodes that have submerged our federal parliament in brutal politicking. In the midst of a scandal involving alleged corruption in 2012, the then member for New England, Tony Windsor, tried to deliver a reality check.
“I make a plea to people,” he said at the time. “Be careful that you do not walk down a road that you regret later on, just for the short-term advantage.”
Fourteen years later, here we are. Things have not improved.

“One bad result can be dismissed as a bad year,” the McKinnon Foundation’s statement said, flagging its coming 2026 democracy index. “When the same problems keep showing up, they become much harder to ignore. And if Australians are continuing to lose confidence in the people and institutions that govern them, we need to understand where that is happening and what is driving it.”

The dangers to democracy aren’t new, nor the risks in ignoring them. The times have only made them worse. We have the statistics, with more arriving, that prove democracy is under challenge and we’ve heard the soulful speeches many times before.
Yet the way politics is practised in this country never seems to change. In the face of such evidence, that really is insanity. •
